speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Money laundering and terrorism financing activities are transboundary in nature.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Illicit funds are the lifeline for international crime and terrorism which impact all countries.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, the Housing Developers (Control and Licensing) Act and the Sale of Commercial Properties Act regulate the sale of housing and commercial properties before completion by developers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Both Acts are administered by the Controller of Housing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are among the series of amendments that Members of this House have made in the last four years to bring Singapore’s anti-money laundering and terrorism financing regime in line with the international standards set out by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: FATF, an intergovernmental body, was established in 1989 to set out national and international standards and promote the effective implementation of measures to combat money laundering and terrorism financing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The FATF Recommendations form part of the broader international financial sector standards and are recognised and used by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank when they conduct assessments of a country’s financial sector.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The FATF Recommendations include measures to be taken under each country's criminal justice and regulatory systems, preventive measures for financial institutions and certain other businesses and professions, and measures to facilitate international cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singapore joined FATF in 1992, and since then we have put in place a very strong legal and regulatory framework to detect, deter and take action against money laundering and terrorism financing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is further complemented by the effective monitoring of implemented initiatives and decisive law enforcement actions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As a responsible member of the international community, Singapore has committed to periodic peer assessments to ensure compliance with the FATF Recommendations, including through changes to legislation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this Bill continues this ongoing effort and will help to strengthen our levers against money laundering and terrorism financing in the real estate sector in line with FATF's direction to strengthen the supervision of non-financial sectors.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, clauses 5 and 10 of the Bill introduce new requirements for developers to facilitate the detection of money laundering and terrorism financing activities.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Developers will need to implement programmes to train their employees and develop internal policies and controls to manage and mitigate money laundering and terrorism financing risks.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Developers should also not open or maintain any account for, or hold and receive monies from, an anonymous source or a buyer with an obviously fictitious name.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill adopts a risk-based approach to anti-money laundering and terrorism financing compliance.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Principal obligations are set out, but businesses will have the flexibility to develop procedures according to the different risks they identify using their own programmes.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, persons who are looking to develop a housing project are required to obtain a housing developer’s licence, and clause 4 of the Bill proposes amendments to give the Controller of Housing power under section 7(1) of the Housing Developers (Control and Licensing) Act, to bar a person who has been convicted of money laundering and terrorism financing offences in Singapore, or has, as a substantial shareholder, or a holder of a responsible position, like partner or director, a person who has been convicted, from being licensed housing developers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will add to the powers the Controller of Housing already has today to refuse, revoke or suspend a housing developer's licence, for cases, such as when the housing developer has been convicted of an offence involving fraud or dishonesty, or when it is carrying on its business in a manner that is detrimental to the interests of its purchasers or to the public.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In addition, amendments in clauses 8 and 10 will disqualify persons convicted of money laundering or terrorism financing offences, from holding responsible positions in developers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Lastly, the Controller of Housing will also be given commensurate enforcement powers to ensure compliance with the new provisions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Under the amendments in clauses 6 and 11 of the Bill, these include powers to require developers to produce relevant information, retain documents and make copies, and disclose information for purposes of investigation and any subsequent criminal proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is in line with penalties introduced in more recent Acts like the Pawnbrokers Act.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It ensures our compliance with the FATF Recommendations and signals our commitment to be a responsible member of the international community.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In addition, the legislative backing will make clear what is necessary and help to ensure more effective enforcement and efficient compliance to these requirements.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I beg to move.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am encouraged to see the whole-of-Government (WOG) effort on anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT).

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Financial institutions have poured substantial resources and investments, including the better use of technology, into improving the effectiveness of AML/CFT measures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Last year’s setting up of the AML/CFT Industry Partnership (ACIP) by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Commercial Affairs Department (CAD), a platform that combines law enforcement and regulatory insight with industry's ground knowledge of business and clients, has helped expand our understanding of emerging risks and typologies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many sectors have put in place the necessary laws to comply with AML/CFT requirements, including lawyers, pawnbrokers and moneylenders.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Therefore, the introduction of the Developers Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing Bill is timely.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The use of real estate to launder illicit funds is an established method of money laundering the world over.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Large sums of illicit funds can be concealed and integrated into the legitimate economy through real estate.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have seen reports where millions of dollars' worth of property have been subject to criminal investigation, when they are suspected to be the proceeds of illicit funds, yet these reported cases are likely to represent only the tip of the iceberg.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is, therefore, critical that we put safeguards in place in the real estate sector to stop it from being a channel for such activities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: My comments on this Bill will focus on effective implementation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst I strongly subscribe to taking an "ecosystem" approach to AML/CFT efforts as we are only as strong as our weakest link, I share the industry’s concerns on the practical limitations on some of the requirements.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Developers are unsure how they can conclusively check and verify a purchaser’s profile, as well as establish purpose of purchase and source of funds, in the course of a sale and purchase transaction.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As current rules on Option to Purchase and Sale and Purchase Agreement only allow cheque, cashier's order or telegraphic transfer, funds flowing into the property sector would have already gone through AML/CFT checks by financial institutions before developers receive them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The option to purchase is not transferable nor assignable, and cash payment is not allowed without the explicit approval of the Controller of Housing.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Also, whether a risk-based approach can be adopted where the levels of checks expected of developers vary according to whether the purchasers are local residents or foreigners, with enhanced checks prescribed for those from high-risk countries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And whether the checks required of other parties in the ecosystem, such as lawyers and real estate agents, can be coordinated so as to reduce duplication and ensure all efforts complement one another.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst the intent of the Bill to stop financial crime in the real estate sector is laudable, we need to ensure that implementation of regulatory measures is not so onerous as to cause the increased cost of compliance to be passed to consumers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To check for suspicious persons and entities, developers need to screen their prospective purchasers against multiple lists provided by relevant authorities, including the United Nation's Sanctions lists.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To assist developers, can the Ministry coordinate and compile a single comprehensive list online to ensure thorough screening against the most updated information?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Under the new regulation, developers are required to appoint a compliance officer, as guided by the MAS notice.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The industry is concerned about the availability of talent to fulfil such a role, as well as its related costs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst I agree there is room to heighten awareness as well as institute measures to check for suspicious property transactions, this burden should not rest only on the shoulders of a compliance officer but those also of the senior management and, indeed, throughout the organisation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Developers should institute a corporate culture that has zero tolerance for money laundering and terrorist financing, and have that communicated rigorously to all staff.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Lessons learnt from experiences of financial institutions should be shared widely so that developers can shorten their learning curve in implementing AML/CFT measures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Such structures help distance the criminal from ownership, with control vested in the hands of third parties to avoid obvious links to true ownership.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We are also subject to the risk of property values being manipulated by criminals buying or selling real estate at prices above or below market value and colluding with others in the ecosystem to "clean" the money.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: One example is when properties are deliberately undervalued and illicit funds are used to pay the difference between the contract price and the properties' true value.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Processes should be in place to question such unusual property price transactions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a member state of FATF, we should support and cooperate with its various recommendations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding, I have some concerns and would like to seek clarifications.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is there a level playing field for all states, especially financial centres?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Ministry qualify "best efforts" and the definition of "negligence"?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, are the measures a continued responsibility or only applicable at the point of the contract, that means, is the developer required to conduct regular checks, periodical checks, before obtaining the Temporary Occupation Permit (TOP) or Certificate of Statutory Completion (CSC)?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At which point in time do the duty and responsibility of the developer end?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is pertinent as the buyer could be a group of investors, fund, trust, public or private company with a variable capital structure and have more than a shareholder or company registered.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The shareholders and investors of these entities could change after the Sale and Purchase.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Bill does not cover properties purchased in the resale market or developments exempted by the Housing Developers Act.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will these regulations apply to a person who has previously been convicted for a similar offence beyond our jurisdiction?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will this legislation only apply to new developers or also target newly appointed directors or new shareholders of existing developers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The terror threat that Singapore faces is at the highest in years.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To keep terrorism at bay, we need a multi-pronged approach.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Apart from shoring up our border security and strengthening social resilience among our citizens, it is important to prohibit any channels of funding terrorism acts.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In doing so, we can help to prevent and deter terrorism activities to a significant extent.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As a member of FATF, it is our obligation to comply with standards set out by the task force.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is for our benefit and safety as well.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Money laundering is the oxygen that gives life to terrorism activities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is also used by other criminals to support their activities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Certainly, this is one of the areas that we have to regulate closely.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, I wonder if we are overreacting and being too heavy-handed in the proposed regulations and duties for developers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I note that under the proposed amendments, developers must implement programmes and measures to prevent money laundering and terrorism financing (ML/TF).

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They must carry out customer due diligence measures, and they are also required to report suspicious transactions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It would be difficult for developers to ascertain the true source of a purchaser's funds, the motives behind the purchase and his relationship or association with a "Politically Exposed Person", as such issues are generally deemed highly personal and private.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Moreover, while developers can screen clients or prospective clients against publicly available lists of individuals and entities known or suspected to be related to a terrorist or a terrorist organisation, such providers cannot be held responsible for the validity and accuracy of such information.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I note with concern that documents and information from due diligence checks must also be retained for a specific time and in a specific form.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Storing and ensuring the security of such data can add up to a costly amount over a long period of time, which leads to increased business costs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How will these programmes be evaluated for their effectiveness?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Considering that these are laymen who lack adequate resources and expertise when it comes to dealing with ML/TF activities, I would not be surprised if some of them slip up and allow ML/TF activities to occur under their very noses without their realising it.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, developers would usually engage third parties like solicitors and licensed estate agents to assist them in the sale of properties.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Would the new regulations mean that these third parties also have to comply with the requirements on due diligence measures?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Who will be held responsible when the measures are found to be inadequate?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the Government wishes for the developers to take on a heavier responsibility, then it must furnish them with the relevant resources and work closely with them to help them come up with the right programmes and execution.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, the Government must not only help with the initial stage, but also with the implementation throughout.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Should there be a weak link somewhere down the line, this can result in serious repercussions and even compromise our national safety.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is not something we should impose on the average citizen.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I urge the Government to reconsider the necessity of the various regulations and their deadlines.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If we look at the existing policies, the risk of transactions being abused for ML/TF activities is frankly not very high.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, I do not see the point of burdening the developers with additional requirements that may or may not serve the purpose of mitigating ML/TF.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The existing standard Option to Purchase (OTP) and Sale and Purchase agreements provide for payment by cheque, cashier's order or telegraphic transfer for residential properties, and the former two payment methods for non-residential properties.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Such funds would necessarily have gone through a financial institution.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Inherent in this payment is that the funds would have gone through AML/CFT by the respective financial institutions before the developers receive them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Should developers wish to provide for an alternative mode of payment, such as cash, they would be required to seek the COH's prior approval.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Developers are "secondary" recipients of funds and the ML/FT risks faced by developers are lower.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Developers are also required to appoint a compliance officer as stated in the MAS Notice.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, the senior management will evaluate decisions to establish business relationships where there are ML/TF suspicions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What requirements would this compliance officer have to fulfil?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can he or she be appointed from the team that conducts these decision evaluations?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Otherwise, this is once again an additional long-term expense for the developers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Moving on to other areas of concern, I note that the developer will not be able to issue the OTP while still being obliged to make a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR).

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: By declining to issue the OTP, this could alert the "customer" that their transactions have raised suspicions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If they are, indeed, involved in ML/TF activities, they may then redirect the funds and it would be difficult to apprehend them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If this turns out to be a mistake, the customer would have missed out on the purchase opportunity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, with regard to ML/TF, there are many more players along the value chain.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are we expecting more amendments to come up?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why do we not amend all relevant Acts at one go?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even more, we should not leave it to the developers to be responsible for ML/TF risk management.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Certainly, everybody has a role to play to combat terrorism.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the Government wishes to have the developers’ full cooperation, then it would be prudent to engage the right people with the relevant know-how to work closely with them and, more importantly, to provide them with the necessary resources to do so, so that it will not end up as just another paper exercise and form signing.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin)   Obviously, it is very important to deter ML/TF.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, the Bill puts too much onus on developers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am afraid that it might increase the cost and even result in negligence.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Do developers have sufficient training to do background checks?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If they use lawyers or agents to sell their properties, are these people required to do background checks on their clients, too?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, banks and other financial institutions have protocols to do background checks on their customers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is it not better to ask them to do the checks?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When a transaction is delayed, innocent customers may lose the opportunity to purchase, and those who are of truly questionable character may smell a rat and, therefore, decide to transfer their funds to somewhere else.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think banks and the Police are most capable of deterring ML/TF.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We may achieve the opposite effect if we demand too much from the developers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Real estate is a popular outlet for illicit funds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Money launderers and terrorism financiers often invest in real estate for the same reasons other people do: the prices are stable, the values generally appreciate over time, and you can live in it or rent it out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill sends a clear message to Singapore's housing developers: you must not be involved with these criminals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They cannot be your customers, your shareholders or your officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: You must take concrete steps to guard against their involvement, and you must report any suspicions you have.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In an interview conducted by The Business Times this February, a housing developer commented that conducting customer due diligence might be, I quote, "quite tricky", for big projects on launch days.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is hard to conduct due diligence when there are so many buyers and so much urgency for everyone involved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The developer said, "The process in the show flat does not quite work that way." Can the Ministry share how developers can best cope with the demands of the new law while not compromising their business operations?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry provide guidelines on how housing developers can adapt to this new law?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It seems to me that this Bill leaves quite a bit of room for housing developers to make their own judgement calls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The word “appropriate” appears 12 times in what is a fairly short bill: appropriate steps, appropriate mechanisms, appropriate arrangements, appropriate measures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The word “adequate” appears seven times: adequate safeguards, adequate programmes and adequate procedures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes these broad guidelines are translated into specific measures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, the Bill states that developers must appoint a compliance officer at the management level.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is useful to companies trying to do the right thing by the law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, more often, the guidelines are left broad.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In section 5C, developers are told they must take appropriate steps to identify, assess and understand the risks in relation to its purchasers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would it be enough to run the purchasers’ names through regulatory searches and sanctions lists?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Or is there a need to commission an investigative firm to dig, expensively, into the background and history of the purchaser?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Numerous other parts of the Bill are written with some ambiguity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At one point, developers are told not to deal with purchasers that have "an obviously fictitious name".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we cannot ask them to significantly increase their costs of doing business while remaining ambiguous about what we want from them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The law should allow a developer, acting in good faith, to confidently say, "I do not need to be fearful of a $100,000 fine." Further to my earlier suggestion to provide housing developers with guidelines, these guidelines could also shed light on what concrete steps developers are required to take to be in compliance with these new requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must remember that we are asking developers who are there to make a profit to do their due diligence which might end up with them making less profits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are asking them to check on their own clients who are paying them and at times paying them a lot of money.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, we need to be more specific, otherwise, these amendments will be futile.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, on this point, can the Minister clarify if the person who is liable for prosecution for failure to do due diligence is actually the person on the ground doing the due diligence?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My concern here is that if a property agent is the one doing the checks and we are going after the director who has never really met the customer, is this going to be effective?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The person who is doing the checks know that he or she is not going to be prosecuted, and the director who might receive hundreds of these reports from hundreds of property agents will never be able to properly do the due diligence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is about other things we can do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government can do more to combat the flow of illicit funds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The unexplained wealth order is one idea that has gained traction in recent years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The authorities can apply to the Courts to issue an unexplained wealth order.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The order would compel an individual suspected of criminal activity to explain how they obtained their assets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The order would allow the authorities to freeze and recover assets if the individuals cannot explain, one, why they own assets worth more than their income and, two, how they have acquired the assets legally.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Several parts of Australia have implemented and actively used this law against those suspected of criminal activity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The United Kingdom introduced the Unexplained Wealth Orders under its Criminal Finance Bill this year and its High Court issued in September the first such order, compelling a jailed Central Asian banker and his wife to explain how they were able to afford an extravagant lifestyle that included ownership of a London mansion and a golf course.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Earlier this month, Malaysia announced that they were also looking into its implementation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill we are reading today tackles the supply side of this problem by regulating our housing developers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I will now address some of the points raised in the course of this debate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I believe Members who have spoken generally agree that as a responsible member of the international community, there is a need for Singapore to do our part to strengthen our levers to effectively detect, deter and prevent ML/TF.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: However, several Members, including Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Ms Foo Mee Har, asked why there was a need to impose these requirements on developers, in particular, since the funds they receive would eventually have to pass through financial institutions and banks which already have to carry out checks anyway.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah is right in that, in general, most ML/TF activities are concentrated in the financial sectors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But as Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Louis Ng said, real estate is also an established method of money laundering worldwide.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, such activities can occur in real estate and real estate can be exposed to questionable practices and be used as a vehicle for ML/TF activities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For the real estate sector, in particular, besides your bankers and lawyers, developers are a key party that deals with property buyers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, they do play an important role in the detection and prevention of such activities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And this is why we are introducing these requirements by amending the two Acts that regulate developers to better facilitate our AML/CTF activities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And this is also the reason why this Bill does not cover transactions involving completed properties because the Bill pertains to the two Acts that regulate the sale of uncompleted housing and commercial properties by developers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are the sale of properties typically sold off-plan and they are exposed to more risks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And our main objective of the Bill is to get developers who are involved in the sale of such uncompleted properties involved in our AML/CFT efforts and to bring them up to the same level as the other players that are involved in real estate transactions, namely, the bankers and the lawyers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For the sale of completed properties, these typically do not involve developers directly and so we rely on the other players in the real estate chain, such as bankers and lawyers, who already have similarly robust obligations under the respective legislation to conduct CDD checks and to report suspicious transactions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, this is really about levelling up and making sure that we cover comprehensively the same requirements, not just on bankers, not just on lawyers, but also now, on real estate developers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why the Bill covers the two Acts that regulate the sale of uncompleted properties.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I understand and I hear the feedback from Members who have spoken and all of you have highlighted and asked if the proposed legislation will be overly onerous on developers, and whether it will impact their business operations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We share the concerns and that is why, in drafting the provisions and in implementing these requirements, we have been careful to implement a calibrated risk-based approach.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in tabling this Bill, we would like to strike a balance between complying with the requirements recommended by FATF and ensuring that the burden on developers is not excessive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why, as I mentioned earlier, the Bill adopts a risk-based approach under which the broad principal obligations are set out.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Perhaps, that is why Mr Louis Ng noted that there are these terminologies which are set out in broad language.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it is deliberately done, so that then businesses have the flexibility to develop procedures according to their business size, customer profile and nationality, and different levels of ML/TF risks which they can identify using their own AML/CTF programmes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will take the time to engage the industry and review these specific requirements before we set them out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That said, I would like to highlight that developers today already collect most of the "Know Your Customer" (KYC) information that we have in mind for the rules.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Any developer that accepts a transaction without doing basic KYC checks will be problematic, even today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I would expect developers today to already collect most of the KYC information that we have in mind for the rules, such as identity documentation, so that incremental compliance costs should not be excessive and should not adversely affect purchasers, especially genuine purchasers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Er Dr Lee also asked how long developers would have to keep records of their diligence checks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And this is consistent with what is prescribed in the FATF recommendations and also in other sectors’ legislations, such as for financial institutions and for pawnbrokers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some Members asked about the extent of the developer's responsibilities in adhering to the requirements of the new Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Specifically, Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about the point at which the developer's duty to monitor their buyers ends, given that the profile of buyers can change after the signing of the sale and purchase agreement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I want to assure Members that we will not be requiring developers to monitor their buyers perpetually.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Instead, the rules will make it clear that the requirements on developers will only apply until the project is completed, which is also the point at which the developer is no longer regulated under the two Acts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Developers should ensure that the information obtained with respect to the purchasers and its beneficial owners is kept updated.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At any point during the monitoring, if the developer comes to know about property which represents proceeds of or is used or intended to be used in connection with, any act which may constitute drug dealing or criminal conduct, the developer will then have to report such suspicious activity to an STRO.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the point is that the rules will not be imposed on the developer perpetually.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Foo Mee Har also asked if developers could rely on third parties, such as estate agents, lawyers or banks, to conduct the necessary checks on their behalf.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Developers will have the flexibility to determine how best to do their checks, including through third parties.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As mentioned, the Bill does adopt a risk-based approach to compliance and we will not rule out the use of such third parties.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But ultimately, the developer bears full responsibility for adhering to the requirements under his new Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the developer should ensure that the third party it hires has the appropriate capabilities and the resources to comply with these measures and are able to provide the relevant information to the developers without delay, upon request, should they decide to use a third party.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Er Dr Lee and Mr Louis Ng asked who specifically would be held responsible if the due diligence measures were found to be inadequate or not complied with.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Foo Mee Har also spoke about the need for the burden of compliance to fall on senior management and throughout the organisation for accountability.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it will really depend on a case-by-case basis, depending on the circumstances.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That officer could be any director, member of the management team, chief executive officer, manager, secretary or other persons acting in such capacity in the developer company.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is also the position taken today under section 27 of the Housing and Developers (Control and Licensing) Act and section 9 of the Sale of Commercial Properties Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Er Dr Lee also asked about the role of the compliance officer that developers must appoint.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This compliance officer can be any appointee at the management level and will be responsible for reviewing the developer's AML/CTF policies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it need not result in additional expense.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the developer must designate a compliance officer and appoint with clear responsibilities for this officer.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Foo Mee Har asked how developers can mitigate the risk brought on by the use of shell companies and other corporate entities to purchase property.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Indeed, the Government is aware of such concerns and we have made legislative amendments to address this issue.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, the Companies Act was amended last year to make the ownership and control of business entities more transparent and thereby reduce opportunities for the misuse of corporate entities for illicit purposes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The FATF recommendations also include requirements for regulated entities to obtain information of beneficial ownership.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in elaborating and crafting the rules, we will make clear the duties of developers in this particular requirement of checking for beneficial ownership as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some Members expressed concern that developers would fail to effectively comply with the new rules due to a lack of understanding of how to implement them or merely go through the motions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Indeed, we do not want this to be a paper exercise or a tick-in-the-box exercise, as some Members have mentioned just now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will be adopting a two-pronged approach to address this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, we want to help developers level up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) will engage the developers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They will do industry outreach and provide all the necessary guidance to developers in the initial implementation stage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Subsequently, URA will provide ongoing support to improve the industry's understanding of what constitutes risky transactions, as well as their risk mitigation capabilities that are needed, in order to foster a good understanding of the new requirements.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked whether other countries have implemented similar regulations, how many, and if there was a level playing field.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Indeed, the whole point of developing international standards under FATF is to ensure that there is a comprehensive global system to fight against ML/TF.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The specific provisions may differ from country to country because even the regulation of the sale of properties varies from country to country.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some countries even prohibit sale of properties off-plan.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But 190 jurisdictions have committed to the FATF recommendations precisely because this is an important international issue and it can make progress through a global effort.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we have the ability to do so, to revoke, suspend or refuse a Licence if the convictions are happening elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is, in fact, a point raised by Mr Murali Pillai yesterday during the debate on the Serious Crimes and Counter Terrorism (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is, in fact, not quite so relevant to this Bill, because, as mentioned by Minister Josephine Teo yesterday, the Government will certainly monitor overseas developments in the area of anti-corruption measures to see if these can be adapted here on another occasion.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Unexplained wealth order legislation has been introduced overseas as an investigation tool to enable enforcement agencies to investigate the source of money.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it is a tool which can and should be capable of being directed at anyone, and not just developers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is really a separate matter outside of the scope of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This Bill is just one of the many changes we are making to our laws to help Singapore be a responsible member of the international community, and to uphold our reputation as a conducive and reputable place to do business.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Failure to impose these AML/CTF requirements across our entire real estate value chain comes at a reputational cost to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I believe that legislative backing will be necessary to ensure effective enforcement and compliance to these requirements.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.31 pm until 3.55 pm.
